extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in analytic methods for integrating linear differential equations (and readers of mathematical problems/solutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and operational rules for integrating linear ordinary (and some partial) differential equations using operator methods (D = d/dx), exponential multipliers, factorization, and substitutions; includes modelling/principle assumptions for applied mechanics problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary operator identities (formulæ A–D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four operator identities involving D (where D denotes d/dx) are established and used constantly to transform and evaluate D^m (x^n y) and related expressions. (The paper lists these four formulae explicitly and remarks they are verified by differentiation and by substitution D^{±k}y for y.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities are the foundational algebraic relations used throughout the method: verify them by direct differentiation or by substituting shifted D-powers for y; changing n into −n converts formula (A) into (B). Similar variants for other shifted powers may be derived and used repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of substitutions y = D^{p} u or y = D^{-p} u to obtain particular integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with an equation of the form (examples given in the paper), set y = D^{p} u (or y = D^{-p} u) to reduce the equation to one in u and thereby obtain particular integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After making the substitution, replace occurrences of D^{k} applied to y by their values from the subsidiary formulae (A)–(B), simplify and drop cancelling terms. If convenient, find particular integrals separately and combine to get the complete integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide by an operating factor and find its effect on the second member (formula (C))
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrating equations where the left-hand side is a product of differential operators (e.g., (φD + β)(ψD + X) y = 0), one may divide first by one factor and determine how that factor acts on the right-hand side by using the exponential/operator manipulation embodied in formula (C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formula (C) to move factors across exponentials and to compute the transformed second member; this permits sequential integration by treating one factor at a time. Keep track that α, β, etc. may be functions of x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncommutativity of differential operator factors — order matters
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot change the order of factors like (φD + β)(ψD + X) without changing the equation, because differential operators with variable coefficients generally do not commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when the product of factors yields the same overall operator whatever the order (for example, when writing via roots of characteristic equation in a special symmetric form) can the order be rearranged without altering the equation; otherwise keep the original order or explicitly account for commutator terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boole's method: factorization via roots of operator polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ(α) has roots r1, r2, …, one may write the operator polynomial as a product (φ(D)+α−r_i) etc., and obtain particular integrals by dividing by all factors but one (without operating on the second member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor the operator polynomial accordingly; each linear factor (0D + X − r_i) y = 0 yields a particular integral. This is a recommended route to obtain a complete integral when the operator polynomial can be factored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting rule with exponentials (formulæ D, E, F): e^{ax} and operator shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplication by exponentials shifts the differential operator: e^{ax} φ(D) e^{-ax} y = φ(D + a) y (and related identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these shifting identities to choose an exponential multiplier that converts the operator into a more convenient form for integration. Formulæ (D),(E),(F) are given and may be applied to transform and integrate more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing exponential multipliers to ease integration
rubrics_metrics.description: By multiplying (or dividing) an equation by an exponential e^{ax} and using the shifting identities one can often make one member easiest to integrate; integrate the simpler member and then undo the multiplier to find y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a so that φ(D + a) simplifies (e.g., reduces order or becomes an integer/polynomial operator). After integrating the transformed equation, invert the exponential multiplier to recover the solution of the original equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When φ(D) is an integer (polynomial) function use operator splitting D = D1 + D2
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ(D) is an integer (polynomial) function, then φ(D)/(x) y (or related expressions) can be handled by letting D1 operate on x only and D2 on y only, expanding φ(D1 + D2) as a finite series (it terminates), and integrating termwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write φ(D) = φ(D1 + D2) = φ(D1) + φ'(D1)D2 + … ; since φ is polynomial, the series terminates and each term separates into a product that can be integrated by known methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of log and multiplicative transformations (formula (G), (H))
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations that replace φ(D) by log φ(D) and y by φ(D) y (or variants) produce operator identities useful for integration, e.g., /{φ0(D)+φ'(D)}y = /{φ0(D);φ}y (notation following paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These transformations can turn one difficult operator equation into an integrable form; follow the constructions illustrated in the text (replace operators by their logarithms where indicated and adjust the dependent variable accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for sequential integration of higher-order equations via operator factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equation that is a product of several first-order operator-factors, integrate sequentially by setting intermediate expressions (e.g., (ψD + X) y = w) and solving the simpler equation (φD + β) w = 0 first, then recovering y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stepwise approach avoids operating across complicated products at once and uses the simpler integrals of lower-order operators to assemble the full solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about changing variables / dropping cancelling terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When substituting (for example y = D^{p}u) and replacing operators using the subsidiary identities, omit terms that cancel and simplify carefully to avoid algebraic mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out the substituted expressions systematically, use the operator identities to replace higher-order terms, and explicitly identify cancelling terms before dividing or integrating to avoid introducing spurious solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to partial differential equations
rubrics_metrics.description: The operator methods and identities developed for ordinary linear differential equations may be applied to certain partial differential equations by analogous manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper asserts such applications are possible and sketches how the same operator algebraic manipulations extend; for PDEs adapt the operator-splitting and exponential-shift techniques as appropriate, checking commutation relations carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical modelling assumptions for rolling/rough-ball problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When modelling a rough ball rolling on an inclined plane, assume: (1) the instantaneous axis of rotation passes through centre of curvature of the path; (2) if ball dimensions ≪ radius of curvature, treat axis as parallel to plane and normal to path; (3) frictional force causing rotation acts opposite the motion and tangential to the path; (4) roughness is sufficient to prevent sliding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions are stated explicitly and must be adopted for the derived differential equations of motion and subsequent approximations (e.g., series expansions, osculation comparisons with parabolic path) to be valid. If any assumption fails (e.g., sliding occurs), the derived conclusions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelling note: include friction when needed to transmit rotation/velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: In problems like an elastic ring on a rotating sphere, friction must be considered; without friction no angular velocity would be communicated to the ring by the rotating sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either include explicit friction terms in the force balance, or (if another force transmits the rotation) state that force and modify equations accordingly. Different physical assumptions lead to different formulae for required angular velocity.
